title: Recall Anchor
user: Anki-style self-learners who know a card only when they can produce a concrete answer, but dislike guessing their own recall rating.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker explicitly questions why flashcard apps make the learner self-rate Good/Average/Bad instead of measuring performance.
An independent builder describes the friction between detailed notes and building long-term memory through active recall.

recurrence: A direct 2025 product complaint plus a separate 2026 active-recall workflow report; the rating decision recurs at every review and can make SRS feel untrustworthy.
current_workaround: Learners select an Anki rating from memory, type a private note elsewhere, or avoid cards that cannot be scored exactly.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki and FSRS schedule reviews well, while RemNote and Quizlet offer basic answer modes; none makes a lightweight evidence trail (typed answer, confidence, and rubric) the unit used to explain the next interval.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for 3 card types: exact text, numeric tolerance, and checklist recall. It records the answer before revealing the key, shows why the suggested interval changed, and exports CSV/Anki fields. Non-goals: generating cards, hosting decks, or diagnosing learning ability.
success_measure: At least 50% of a 20-user pilot completes 100 anchored reviews in two weeks and reports fewer manual rating changes than with their prior deck.
monetization: one-time — personal study data should remain local and the utility has durable, individual value.
constraints: Local-first encrypted export; no sensitive educational records or biometric claims; support Unicode and accessible keyboard-only review.
why_distinct: It improves the decision between recall and scheduling rather than being another flashcard library or an LLM card generator.

title: Run Before Next
user: People learning programming from video lessons who need to prove they can alter and run the idea before continuing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Scrimba reports nearly two million users of editable, runnable video lessons and says learners wanted full-stack environments beyond browser-only frontend examples.
A widely discussed learner account describes coding practice as confusing, frustrating, and dependent on working through failure rather than syntax alone.

recurrence: An established interactive-course provider reports scale and a separate 2025 learner discussion emphasizes the failure/feedback gap; passive completion remains a persistent problem.
current_workaround: Pause a video, recreate files in a local editor, copy a final repository, or rely on course quizzes disconnected from runnable code.
incumbents_and_gap: Scrimba, Codecademy, and Replit provide full course platforms; a small creator or documentation author lacks a portable way to attach one falsifiable code checkpoint to an existing lesson.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension and tiny author manifest that pauses selected video timestamps, opens a prebuilt sandbox, and requires one test or output change before resume. Non-goals: video hosting, course marketplace, accounts, or AI code completion.
success_measure: In a pilot lesson, 70% of learners finish at least three checkpoints and 60% can pass the final changed-input test without replaying the preceding segment.
monetization: freemium — free local manifests encourage creator adoption; paid classroom analytics can remain optional.
constraints: Only run allowlisted sandbox templates; do not scrape or redistribute video; obey host CSP and avoid storing learner source code by default.
why_distinct: The product is a narrow, embeddable verification layer for existing lessons, not another video course or online IDE.

title: Seeded ML Drills
user: Self-taught ML practitioners who want short, reproducible model-building exercises and immediate checks without inventing a project or asking an assistant for the answer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker requests a LeetCode-like ML resource with standardized questions, quick feedback, and runnable PyTorch exercises rather than a custom project.
A separate developer discussion argues that the journey and understanding matter more than simply arriving at generated code.

recurrence: A direct request for standardized ML practice and an independent concern about AI bypassing understanding in 2025; the gap is acute for learners outside a course.
current_workaround: Follow notebooks, copy Kaggle examples, build an oversized portfolio project, or ask an LLM to create and then explain an exercise.
incumbents_and_gap: Kaggle, DeepLearning.AI, LeetCode, and Google Colab have content or execution, but do not focus on seeded, deterministic, concept-sized training traces with a locally checkable result.
smallest_useful_product: Static web lab with 30 NumPy/PyTorch drills, fixed datasets/seeds, hidden assertions, and a replayable run record. Non-goals: leaderboards, model hosting, interview scoring, or an AI tutor.
success_measure: At least 40% of new users complete five distinct drills in one week, with 75% of completed runs reproducible from their exported record.
monetization: free — open exercise formats and local reproducibility are more valuable than paywalling foundational practice.
constraints: Use permissively licensed toy datasets; execute in a browser sandbox; make all expected outputs and grading limitations transparent.
why_distinct: It is deliberate practice around model behavior, not a generic coding challenge site or a chat wrapper that supplies solutions.

title: Show Your Debugging
user: Beginning developers using AI coding tools who need a lightweight practice constraint that preserves independent diagnosis and debugging skill.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The discussion frames a new form of 'vibe code hell' replacing tutorial hell and commenters specifically worry about tools masking skills AI cannot teach.
A developer explicitly describes recovering from over-reliance on AI and the loss of ordinary problem-solving habits.

recurrence: Independent 2025–26 accounts describe the same learning failure: code completes but the learner cannot reconstruct the reasoning; severity rises as AI becomes default in beginner tooling.
current_workaround: Turn off AI entirely, use a paper notebook, or accept generated patches and hope later repetition creates understanding.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Codeium optimize delivery, while Exercism offers exercises; neither turns a learner's hypothesis, failed test, and repair into a short reviewable practice artifact inside an ordinary editor.
smallest_useful_product: VS Code extension that asks for a one-line hypothesis before reveal, captures test output and the learner's chosen fix, then produces a local 'debugging receipt' for review. Non-goals: code generation, surveillance, grading, or disabling assistants.
success_measure: Pilot learners independently repair 20% more repeated bug patterns after four weeks than a baseline set with no trace review.
monetization: free — the format needs broad classroom and self-learner adoption; optional educator export can follow.
constraints: Local-only source/test capture by default; never transmit proprietary code; clearly describe that receipts evidence process, not competence.
why_distinct: It is a learner-owned reflection tool that works alongside AI rather than another AI coding assistant.

title: Proof Pact
user: Independent Lean 4 learners who need a structured, accountable way to work through proof exercises with another person instead of collecting disconnected tutorials.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN requester says it is difficult to find a structured instructor-led Lean 4 course or organized study group, as opposed to documentation and tutorials.
The article distinguishes final answers from rigorous proofs and reports that difficult proof reasoning remains a meaningful gap for current AI.

recurrence: A direct 2025 request for study structure and a separate proof-focused discussion show that proof explanation—not just final output—remains valuable.
current_workaround: Work through Mathlib docs alone, join a large Discord, or use an LLM to suggest proof steps without a stable peer routine.
incumbents_and_gap: Lean's documentation, Zulip, and natural-number-game offer resources; they do not provide a tiny recurring pair protocol that commits both learners to a theorem, a failed attempt, and an explanation.
smallest_useful_product: Web app creates a two-person weekly pact from public Lean exercises, assigns complementary roles, records proof-state snapshots, and exports a Markdown session note. Non-goals: matching strangers at scale, solving proofs with AI, course hosting, or grading.
success_measure: At least 30% of matched pairs complete three weekly sessions and each submits two independently explained proof attempts in a month.
monetization: free — a small open study utility needs a low-friction community; paid private cohorts are a possible later service.
constraints: Use only openly licensed/public exercise links; obtain consent for partner-visible notes; no claims that a proof is pedagogically correct beyond Lean's checker.
why_distinct: It organizes deliberate peer proof work rather than creating another tutorial catalogue or theorem-proving chatbot.

title: Learn Ledger
user: Self-directed learners pursuing a multi-week skill who need to see whether their reading, practice, and projects actually produced usable evidence of progress.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A large discussion asks where self-directed learners are and debates how people sustain learning outside institutional pathways.
The article promotes open-source project work as a way to turn undirected time into visible career evidence.

recurrence: A broad 2025 self-directed-learning thread and a separate practical project-oriented account both point to the missing bridge between consuming resources and demonstrating progress.
current_workaround: Keep a bookmark pile, a Notion dashboard, scattered Git commits, and an end-of-month memory of what was learned.
incumbents_and_gap: Notion, Obsidian, and GitHub Projects store plans and artifacts; they do not make an intentionally small learning claim linked to practice evidence and a next retrieval date the primary object.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first web notebook where each goal has a claim, source link, practice artifact, self-check, and scheduled revisit; export one-page evidence maps. Non-goals: social feed, certificates, AI summaries, or a universal knowledge graph.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 60% of active users attach evidence to at least six learning claims and reopen at least three scheduled reviews.
monetization: one-time — personal learning records should be portable and useful without recurring cloud rent.
constraints: Local-first by default; URLs/artifacts may be private; provide encrypted export and no employability or credential claims.
why_distinct: It is an evidence-and-retrieval ledger, not another notes app, habit tracker, or public portfolio builder.

title: Math Missing Step
user: Adults returning to mathematics for technical study who need to locate the one prerequisite idea blocking a problem without restarting an entire curriculum.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants to relearn math and asks which earlier experiences and roadmap decisions mattered; replies span forgotten fundamentals and goal-specific pathways.
A 2026 explainer deliberately pauses an ML sequence to rebuild slope from first principles before advancing.

recurrence: The 2025 request and a separate 2026 basic-concept detour show a recurring need to repair a narrowly missing foundation rather than consume a full linear course.
current_workaround: Search YouTube, jump among Khan Academy playlists, restart a textbook chapter, or ask a chatbot for an explanation with uncertain prerequisites.
incumbents_and_gap: Khan Academy, Brilliant, and Math Academy provide broad curricula; they do not offer a transparent, user-authored dependency sketch tied to the exact failed transformation in a problem.
smallest_useful_product: Static interactive tool with a curated algebra-to-calculus prerequisite graph, one diagnostic prompt per node, and printable 'repair path' cards. Non-goals: adaptive tutoring, automated proof grading, full video lessons, or grade prediction.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users identify a three-node-or-shorter repair path and correctly solve a matched transfer problem within 30 minutes.
monetization: free — transparent prerequisite maps benefit from review and remixing; optional subject packs can fund maintenance.
constraints: Have math educators review content; label diagnostics as guidance rather than diagnosis; use openly licensed examples and accessible MathML rendering.
why_distinct: It finds and repairs a local conceptual gap instead of competing as a complete adaptive math platform.

title: Deadline Reality Check
user: Students with several overlapping assignments who need a believable reschedule plan after they miss a work block, not another idealized calendar.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Ocal creator says students struggle with the cognitive overhead of estimating task duration and fitting assignments into real schedules, not simply with motivation.
A student workflow account describes assignments as messy and emphasizes understanding, staged work, and avoiding hurried or copied submissions.

recurrence: Two separate 2025 reports characterize planning overhead and rushed work as the problem; a missed session can cascade into cramming and copied work.
current_workaround: Manually drag calendar blocks, rewrite to-do lists, hide overdue tasks, or work late without re-estimating downstream consequences.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Calendar, Todoist, MyStudyLife, and Ocal schedule tasks; they do not foreground a plain-language receipt of what must move, what can be shortened, and which deadline becomes at risk after one actual miss.
smallest_useful_product: Local calendar importer where a learner enters task chunks and marks one block missed; it proposes a constrained reschedule and emits an honest risk receipt. Non-goals: LMS scraping, AI-generated coursework, social accountability, or grade forecasting.
success_measure: In a two-week pilot, 60% of users reschedule an interrupted plan within five minutes and complete at least one task before its revised risk date.
monetization: one-time — students need a dependable personal utility without a recurring planning subscription.
constraints: Use local calendar data or explicit ICS imports only; no institutional credentials; make uncertainty and user-entered estimates visible.
why_distinct: It is an after-the-plan failure-recovery tool, not another task list or AI calendar assistant.

title: Keep the Sentence
user: Language learners reading real web content who need to save a word together with its original context, meaning, and later retrieval cue without breaking reading flow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The builder describes repeatedly interrupting book reading to look up, contextualize, and later manually turn vocabulary into exercises; commenters request SRS and audio.
An independent builder reports that opening a new tab, pasting text into a translator, or translating the whole page disrupts reading and loses original context.

recurrence: Independent 2025 and 2026 builders report the same context-loss and tab-switching cost; this happens at every unfamiliar word in authentic reading.
current_workaround: Use browser translate, copy words into Anki, take screenshots, or save an isolated dictionary definition.
incumbents_and_gap: Readlang, LingQ, Language Reactor, Google Translate, and Anki each cover portions of the flow; the gap is a local, source-preserving capture that queues retrieval without becoming a paid reader or content platform.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension saves selected phrase, surrounding two sentences, URL/title, language, and a learner-written gloss; a daily offline review asks for the phrase in that exact context. Non-goals: machine translation service, scraped content library, generated exercises, or account requirement.
success_measure: At least 50% of captured phrases are reviewed once within seven days and 70% of users say capture took under ten seconds without leaving the page.
monetization: one-time — local capture/export is a personal utility and should not meter a learner's reading.
constraints: Store only user-selected snippets; respect page permissions and copyright; do not redistribute source text; local encryption and Anki CSV export.
why_distinct: The twist is retaining the learner's own source sentence and retrieval history, rather than another translator, flashcard app, or AI-generated vocabulary feed.

title: Hear the Difference
user: Adult language learners who can recognize a word but freeze when producing its sound, tone, or minimal-pair distinction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A pronunciation-scoring launch immediately receives a request for language coverage, showing that learners need support beyond a single assumed language.
The author says flashcards enabled recognition but not speaking Chinese with the right pinyin and tones, motivating typing/hearing practice.

recurrence: A 2025 learner report and a 2026 pronunciation-tool discussion identify a production-vs-recognition gap and multilingual coverage as unresolved needs.
current_workaround: Repeat isolated audio, use a generic speech score, record voice notes, or return to flashcards that do not reveal which sound distinction was missed.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo, Speechling, ELSA Speak, and general ASR offer drills or scores; they rarely preserve a small learner-owned history of confusable contrasts and the correction that worked.
smallest_useful_product: Mobile web recorder for curated minimal pairs and tone pairs: listen, speak, tag what was confused, then replay a spaced contrast set. Non-goals: accent diagnosis, fluency scoring, live tutoring, or unrestricted speech surveillance.
success_measure: After ten sessions, pilot learners improve at least 20 percentage points on a blinded minimal-pair recognition-and-production check for their selected contrast.
monetization: freemium — a free offline core builds trust; optional downloadable language contrast packs can fund curation.
constraints: Voice recordings are sensitive: local storage and explicit deletion are mandatory; never claim clinical/accent correctness; use licensed recordings or user voice only.
why_distinct: It focuses on durable learner-selected confusions and comparative listening, not a black-box pronunciation grade.

title: Work Log Check
user: Teachers assigning take-home work in the chatbot era who need a humane way to see a student's process without webcam proctoring or AI-detection claims.

evidence.quote_or_summary: University instructors discuss how old exam formats fail when chatbots are readily available and describe growing dependence on LLMs as a crutch.
A technical lab instructor built a LAN-only assessment system after unreliable infrastructure disrupted final exams, highlighting operational constraints alongside integrity concerns.

recurrence: Two 2026 educator accounts show simultaneous pressure from AI-authorship uncertainty and fragile classroom infrastructure; high-stakes proctoring is not an acceptable default.
current_workaround: Use invasive proctoring, unreliable AI detectors, oral defenses for everyone, or ignore process and grade only a polished final artifact.
incumbents_and_gap: Turnitin, Proctorio, Google Classroom, and Moodle cover plagiarism, surveillance, or submission; they do not offer a small offline-capable, student-curated process receipt that never claims to detect AI use.
smallest_useful_product: Local-first assignment journal that lets students attach timestamped planning notes, intermediate exports, source citations, and a two-minute self-explanation; teachers receive a concise receipt. Non-goals: AI detection, keystroke logging, webcam monitoring, or replacing an LMS.
success_measure: In a classroom pilot, teachers can review a receipt in under two minutes and 75% of students say it made their work process clearer without feeling monitored.
monetization: freemium — individual/student use should remain free; institutions can pay for managed class spaces and retention controls.
constraints: FERPA/GDPR-sensitive educational records; explicit retention/deletion policy; no covert telemetry; offline export and accessibility are requirements.
why_distinct: It documents a learner's chosen evidence of process instead of pretending to infer authorship from writing or surveillance data.

title: Steady Take
user: Beginning instrumentalists practicing short technical passages who need feedback on repeatability and control, not only whether they hit notes or played fast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A long-running sight-reading app is praised by a learner; commenters ask for instrument-specific expansion, showing demand for focused practice tools.
The builder argues that fast or accurate notes can still sound unstable and identifies timing wobble as the neglected practice signal.

recurrence: A 2025 learner response and a 2026 builder's focused measurement problem both support a lasting niche: feedback on controllable repetition rather than gamified speed.
current_workaround: Use a metronome, record phone audio, replay takes manually, or chase a game's score without seeing whether timing variance improved.
incumbents_and_gap: Simply Piano, Yousician, Tonara, and metronome apps offer lessons, note accuracy, or practice logs; few make a six-to-eight repetition stability trend from a learner-selected passage the central feedback loop.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA microphone/MIDI practice timer that records onset timing across repeated short patterns, visualizes variance, and lets a learner mark a take as controlled. Non-goals: song library, transcription, social leaderboards, AI composition, or performance grading.
success_measure: After three weeks, 60% of active users reduce timing variance by 15% on one saved passage and complete six repeat sessions.
monetization: one-time — a focused practice instrument has enduring individual value and should work without an account.
constraints: Audio remains on device; disclose microphone limitations; no claims of professional assessment; use Web MIDI opportunistically and preserve a no-MIDI mode.
why_distinct: It measures repeatable control in a learner's own exercise, rather than becoming a content catalogue, rhythm game, or black-box music tutor.
